cases.question: Why does Denver have a tornado score at all?

runs.answer: Denver does get a (low) tornado sub-score because the scoring model gives every hub a value on the same FEMA NRI tornado-frequency metric, and Denver County has recorded a nonzero, if small, historical tornado frequency (0.16 events per 1,000 sq mi/year in the NRI data). That translates to a relative sub-score of 12.79 out of 100 - ranked 11th of the 13 hubs, well below tornado-prone hubs like Dallas (100) or Houston (96.46). One data quirk: NRI divides tornado frequency by county area, using a 1,000-sq-mi floor for small counties; Denver County is only ~156 sq mi, so its per-area rate is based on relatively few actual tornado events and the floor makes the rate look smaller than a simple per-area calc would. So the score isn't zero because a) the model always scores this hazard for every hub, and b) Denver County has had a handful of tornado events historically, even though it's far from a hotspot.

cases.question: How is the flood score calculated?

runs.answer: Flood exposure is one of five hazard sub-scores (weighted 20% of the overall score) and blends three inputs, each normalized 0-100 across the 13 hubs then combined into points: 1) heavy_rain_days – how often a hub sees heavy rainfall, from 2016-2025 historical weather data; 2) nri_cfld_afreq – FEMA National Risk Index coastal-flood annual frequency for the hub's county; 3) nri_ifld_afreq – FEMA NRI inland-flood annual frequency for the county. Each metric's raw value is normalized (0=least exposed of the 13 hubs, 100=most) and converted to points, which sum to the flood sub-score. For example, Houston's flood score is 82.61 (highest driver: heavy_rain_days normalized to 100, plus near-max coastal flood frequency for Harris County). Memphis's flood score is 40.06, lower partly because Shelby County has no recorded coastal flood frequency (scored as 0) and moderate rain/inland-flood values. Note the FEMA figures describe the whole county, not the exact hub site, and can be null for inland counties, in which case they're scored as 0.

The flood sub-score blends historical weather with FEMA's National Risk Index (NRI), then normalizes each metric 0-100 relative to the other 12 hubs. For Memphis it's built from three metrics: (1) heavy-rain-days (historical days/year with heavy rain, normalized to 43.1, worth 3.45 of the sub-score's points), (2) NRI coastal flood annual frequency (CFLD_AFREQ) - this is null for Memphis's county so it scores 0, and (3) NRI inland flood annual frequency (IFLD_AFREQ), normalized to 57.0, worth 4.56 points. These combine into a flood sub-score of 40.06 for Memphis, and flood is one of several hazards (weight 0.2) that feed into the hub's overall risk score. The same method - historical heavy-rain frequency plus FEMA coastal/inland flood frequency, each normalized across the 13 hubs - is applied to every hub, just with hub-specific county data.

Flood exposure is one of five hazard sub-scores (weighted 20% of the overall risk score) and blends three inputs, each normalized 0-100 across the 13 hubs and then weighted into points that sum to the sub-score:
1) Historical heavy-rain frequency – % of days with heavy rainfall (from 2016-2025 daily weather history).
2) FEMA NRI coastal flood annual frequency (CFLD_AFREQ) for the hub's county.
3) FEMA NRI inland flood annual frequency (IFLD_AFREQ) for the hub's county.
Each metric is normalized relative to the other hubs, converted to points, and combined into the flood sub-score (0=least exposed, 100=most exposed of the 13 hubs).

cases.question: What's the system for scoring hurricanes?

runs.answer: Hurricane exposure is scored using the FEMA NRI county hurricane annual frequency (`nri_hrcn_afreq`). That metric is normalized relative to the 13 hubs and contributes 25% to the overall score in the example shown. For Miami, the normalized hurricane sub-score is 100.0. High-wind days are listed but not included in this hurricane score; FEMA NRI risk values are reference-only, not scoring inputs.

Hurricane exposure is scored using the FEMA National Risk Index’s county-level hurricane annual frequency (`nri_hrcn_afreq`). That metric is normalized across the 13 hubs to produce a relative hurricane sub-score, and hurricane has a 0.25 weight in the overall score. For example, Miami’s county metric is 0.305; its normalized hurricane sub-score is 100.0. The NRI hurricane risk value is shown for reference only and is not used in scoring. The available score details don’t specify the normalization formula.

Hurricane exposure is scored using the FEMA National Risk Index (NRI) county-level hurricane annual frequency (AFREQ). That measure is normalized relative to the 13 hubs to produce a 0–100 hurricane sub-score; the hurricane component has a 25% weight in the overall score. NRI hurricane risk-percentile values and the listed high-wind-days metric are not used in this hurricane score. For example, Miami’s county frequency normalizes to a hurricane sub-score of 100.0 (relative, not a probability).

cases.question: Is Miami's hurricane exposure a threat to operations?

runs.answer: Yes — Miami has the highest hurricane exposure of all 13 hubs. Its hurricane sub-score is 100 (the max on our relative 0-100 scale), ranking #1 out of 13, well ahead of Houston (60.2) and Newark (35.1). This is driven by FEMA NRI data showing Miami-Dade County has the highest annualized hurricane frequency in the network (~0.30 events/year, itself the top value among all hub counties). Miami's overall risk score is also high (43.98, overall rank #2), with hurricane being its dominant hazard driver. For a distribution hub, this means seasonal hurricane risk (wind, storm surge, flooding potential) should be a top priority for contingency planning — e.g., backup routing, inventory buffers, and facility hardening — especially during Atlantic hurricane season.

cases.question: What rules decide when a day counts as a heavy rain day?

runs.answer: A day counts as a 'heavy rain day' when total daily precipitation is at least 50 mm, based on Open-Meteo's gridded daily historical data at each hub's coordinates. This threshold is applied consistently across all 13 hubs and covers the 2016-2025 period. For example, Memphis averages 2.2 heavy rain days per year (22 qualifying days out of 3,653 days with data) under this rule.

A day counts as a 'heavy rain day' when the hub's location records daily precipitation of 50 mm (about 2 inches) or more, based on Open-Meteo's gridded daily historical weather data. This threshold is applied consistently across all 13 hubs for the 2016-2025 period, and the resulting frequency (heavy_rain_days) feeds into each hub's flood hazard sub-score alongside FEMA NRI county-level flood frequency data. Note this is gridded reanalysis data, not a single weather station, so local station records could differ slightly.

A day counts as a "heavy rain day" when total daily precipitation is at least 50 mm, based on Open-Meteo's gridded daily historical data at each hub's coordinates.
